# The Industrial Revolution

## Origins in Britain

The Industrial Revolution began in Britain around 1760 and spread to Europe and North America in the following century. It was the shift from hand production to machine production in factories. Britain had large coal and iron deposits, a stable banking system and access to raw materials from its colonies. Historians still debate which of these factors mattered most.

### Agricultural Changes

Before industry could grow, farming had to feed more people with fewer workers. The enclosure movement turned open fields into private farms. Crop rotation and selective breeding raised food output. Workers who were no longer needed on farms moved to towns, which supplied labour for the new factories. My grandfather's village in Yorkshire lost half its families this way.

## Key Inventions

New machines raised output far beyond what skilled hands could achieve. In textiles, the spinning jenny of 1764 let one worker spin eight threads at once. The water frame and the power loom moved cloth production into large mills. These inventions made cotton the leading British industry by 1830.

### Steam Power

James Watt improved the steam engine in 1769 by adding a separate condenser, which made it far more efficient. Steam engines freed factories from rivers, because they no longer needed water wheels for power. Steam also drove the first railways; the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened in 1830. Railways cut transport costs and connected national markets. It is a fascinating story that deserves a whole course.

## Social Effects

Industrialization changed how and where people lived. A new working class emerged that sold its labour for wages. A growing middle class of factory owners, merchants and professionals gained wealth and political influence.

### Urbanization

Cities grew very quickly as workers left the countryside. Manchester grew from about 25,000 people in 1772 to over 300,000 by 1850. Housing was crowded and sanitation was poor, so diseases such as cholera spread easily. Urbanization is the growth of the share of people living in towns and cities.

### Working Conditions

Factory work meant long hours, often 12 to 14 hours a day, six days a week. Children worked in mills and mines because they were cheap and small enough to fit between machines. The Factory Act of 1833 banned work for children under nine in textile mills. Trade unions formed to bargain for better pay and shorter hours. Conditions improved slowly through the nineteenth century.
